paper_title: Physiological effects of visual stimulation with full-scale wall images composed of vertically and horizontally arranged wooden elements
abstract: Wood is a raw material that is used not only in the production of structural members for various buildings, but also in the interior finishes that are directly seen and touched by the occupants. Wood has also been recognized as a human-friendly material, but few studies have experimentally confirmed the physiological benefits it brings to humans. Therefore, the aim of the present study was to investigate the physiological effects of visual stimulation with wood. Two types of full-scale square, wooden-wall images composed of vertically or horizontally arranged lumber, were prepared using computer graphics and projected onto a large display to create the visual stimuli, and a gray image was also prepared as a control. Twenty-eight female Japanese university students participated in the study. The participants initially spent 60 s viewing the gray background (rest period) and then observed each of the wooden-wall images and the gray image separately in a random order for 90 s each. During the visual stimulation, the oxyhemoglobin (oxy-Hb) concentration as an indicator of prefrontal brain activity and heart rate variability as an indicator of autonomic nervous activity were continuously measured in each participant. Subjective evaluation of each visual stimulus was then performed using a modified semantic differential method and the Profile of Mood States 2nd Edition test. It was found that visual stimulation with either of the wooden interior wall images induced a significant decrease in oxy-Hb concentration in the left and right prefrontal cortex compared with the gray image. Furthermore, the subjective evaluation showed that the wooden-wall images provided a significantly more “comfortable,” “relaxed,” and “natural” impression than the gray image and decreased the negative mood states, with the vertically arranged wooden-wall image having a more positive effect than the horizontally arranged image.
methodology: The study employed a within-subjects experimental design in an artificial climate chamber (24 °C, 50% relative humidity, 50 lx illumination). Participants viewed visual stimuli projected onto a 4K-compatible high-vision liquid-crystal display (1053 mm x 1053 mm, 1.1 m viewing distance) in a dark room. The protocol involved a 60-s rest period (gray background) followed by 90-s visual stimulation periods for each of the three stimuli (vertical wood, horizontal wood, gray control) in a random order. Physiological responses were continuously measured, followed by subjective evaluations. Near-infrared time-resolved spectroscopy (TRS) was used to measure oxyhemoglobin (oxy-Hb) concentration in the left and right prefrontal cortex (Fp1 and Fp2 positions) at 1 Hz. Heart rate variability (HRV) and heart rate were measured using a portable electrocardiograph (Activtracer AC-301A) at 1 kHz, with LF and HF components calculated by the maximum-entropy method and natural logarithmic transformation applied. Psychological measurements included a modified semantic differential (SD) method (13-point scale, 4 adjective pairs: comfortable-uncomfortable, relaxed-awakening, natural-artificial, varied-ordered) and the Profile of Mood States 2nd Edition (POMS 2) test (35 questions, 7 mood subscales: T-A, D-D, A-H, F-I, C-B, V-A, F, and TMD score). Statistical analysis involved paired t-tests with Holm correction for physiological data and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction for psychological data, with p < 0.05 considered significant.
sample: 28 female Japanese university students (mean age: 22.3 ± 2.1 years; mean height: 158.8 ± 6.0 cm; mean weight: 51.9 ± 5.9 kg). Participants who smoked, had any disease, or were menstruating during the study period were excluded.
manipulated_features: Vertical wooden-wall image (full-scale, square, composed of vertically arranged Japanese cedar lumber, 2160x2160 pixels)
Horizontal wooden-wall image (full-scale, square, composed of horizontally arranged Japanese cedar lumber, 2160x2160 pixels, created by rotating the vertical image 90°)
Gray image (control, same brightness as wooden-wall images, 2160x2160 pixels)
outcomes: Oxyhemoglobin (oxy-Hb) concentration in left prefrontal cortex (TRS)
Oxyhemoglobin (oxy-Hb) concentration in right prefrontal cortex (TRS)
High-frequency (HF) power of HRV (parasympathetic nervous activity)
Low-frequency to high-frequency (LF/HF) ratio of HRV (sympathetic nervous activity)
key_findings: Visual stimulation with either vertical or horizontal wooden-wall images induced a significant decrease in oxy-Hb concentration in both the left and right prefrontal cortex compared to the gray image (p<0.05).
Overall mean oxy-Hb concentrations in left prefrontal cortex: vertical image = -0.16 ± 0.09 µM, horizontal image = 0.04 ± 0.10 µM, gray image = 0.46 ± 0.14 µM.
Overall mean oxy-Hb concentrations in right prefrontal cortex: vertical image = -0.14 ± 0.09 µM, horizontal image = 0.03 ± 0.09 µM, gray image = 0.35 ± 0.11 µM.
No significant difference in oxy-Hb concentration was found between vertical and horizontal wooden-wall images.
No significant differences were found in HF value, LF/HF ratio, or heart rate among the three visual stimuli.
Participants reported significantly more 'comfortable,' 'relaxed,' 'natural,' and 'varied' feelings after observing wooden-wall images compared to the gray image (p<0.05 for all).
Observation of the vertical wooden-wall image evoked a significantly more 'relaxed' feeling than both the horizontal wooden-wall image and the gray image (p<0.05).
Negative mood state scores (D-D, F-I, T-A subscales) were significantly lower for wooden-wall images than for the gray image (p<0.05).
C-B subscale score was significantly lower for the vertical wooden-wall image than for the gray image (p<0.05).
T-A subscale score was significantly lower for the vertical wooden-wall image than for the horizontal wooden-wall image (p<0.05).
Positive mood state scores (V-A, F subscales) were significantly higher for wooden-wall images than for the gray image (p<0.05).
Positive mood state scores (V-A, F subscales) were significantly higher for the vertical wooden-wall image compared to the horizontal wooden-wall image (p<0.05).

Total Mood Disturbance (TMD) score was significantly lower for wooden-wall images than for the gray image (p<0.05), and significantly lower for the vertical wooden-wall image than for the horizontal wooden-wall image (p<0.05).
The vertical wooden-wall image was evaluated as being slightly 'varied' (neither 'ordered' nor excessively 'varied').
theories_referenced: General concept of positive psychological and physiological effects of the natural environment on humans [1-3]
Relationship between pleasant/unpleasant feelings and oxy-Hb concentrations [49]
mechanisms: The study suggests that visual stimulation with wooden-wall images calms prefrontal cortex activities, which is associated with positive psychological responses. The mechanism for brain activity is based on the principle that increased local brain activity leads to increased blood flow, exceeding oxygen consumption, thus increasing oxy-Hb concentration. Conversely, a decrease in oxy-Hb indicates reduced brain activity, interpreted as a calming effect. The study also notes that pleasant feelings decrease oxy-Hb concentrations, while unpleasant feelings increase them, linking the observed physiological calming to positive subjective evaluations.
limitations: Unclear whether significant oxy-Hb decrease occurs in the right, left, or both prefrontal cortices, requiring further investigation.
Visual stimulation might have been insufficient to induce significant changes in autonomic nervous activities (HRV and heart rate).
Potential impact of factors like spectral characteristics of the large display, type of grain pattern, and magnitude of grain pattern contrast on results needs further verification.
The mechanism causing different physiological and psychological effects between vertical and horizontal wood arrangements is currently unknown and requires further experimental design.
All participants were female, so findings may not generalize to males, necessitating additional studies with male participants.
design_implications: Visual stimulation with wood in interior spaces can induce physiological and psychological relaxation.

The arrangement of wooden elements (e.g., vertical vs. horizontal) in interior walls can significantly influence the strength and type of positive effects on occupants, with vertical arrangements potentially leading to greater relaxation and positive mood states.
